findings.summary: The claim that an unused type parameter produces no warning without a lint rule is false — tsc reports it under noUnusedParameters.
findings.evidence: "Unused T becomes unknown; no warning without a lint rule." But TypeScript 5.9.3's checker has `checkUnusedTypeParameters`, which emits `_0_is_declared_but_its_value_is_never_read` (TS6133) with kind `Parameter`, gated on `compilerOptions.noUnusedParameters` (`case 1 /* Parameter */: return !!compilerOptions.noUnusedParameters`); with several unused params it emits "All type parameters are unused". The language service also surfaces it as an unused-identifier suggestion (greyed out) with no flag at all.
findings.fix: Change to: "Unused T becomes `unknown`; `noUnusedParameters` reports it (TS6133), and editors grey it out by default — no lint rule needed."

findings.summary: The rule given for conflicting inference candidates is wrong: for argument inference TypeScript picks a common supertype and errors when none exists, it does not form a union.
findings.evidence: "Conflicting candidates union instead of erroring." (page 3, section "2. Steering Inference"). In TypeScript 5.9.3 `getCovariantInference` does `inference.priority & PriorityImpliesCombination ? getUnionType(baseCandidates, Subtype) : getCommonSupertype(baseCandidates)`, and `getSingleCommonSupertype` reduces to a single candidate — so `declare function two<T>(a: T, b: T): T; two(1, "x")` infers `T = number` and reports "Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'number'". Only literals sharing a base type combine (`two(1, 2)` → `1 | 2`), and the union rule the slide states is the `infer` rule the deck already gives correctly on page 4 ("Covariant sites union, contravariant sites intersect").
findings.fix: Replace the bullet with: "Candidates collapse to a common supertype; same-base literals union (`1 | 2`), truly conflicting ones error." Keep "covariant sites union" scoped to multiple `infer` candidates.

findings.summary: "tail-eliminated" is used as a budget category without ever being defined or exemplified anywhere in the part.
findings.evidence: Page 1 table row ["tail-eliminated","~1000"], repeated on page 4 as "Budget: depth ~50, ~1000 with tail recursion." No block in the part says what makes a recursive conditional type tail-recursive.
findings.fix: Add one line beside the limits table defining the term with a minimal example — e.g. an accumulator-passing recursion `type Rev<T extends unknown[], Acc extends unknown[] = []> = T extends [infer H, ...infer R] ? Rev<R, [H, ...Acc]> : Acc`, where the recursive call is the entire branch.

findings.summary: "never in, never out" is presented as a universal rule immediately under the tuple-wrapped conditional, where it does not hold — the rule applies only to distributive (naked) type parameters.
findings.evidence: "type NonEmpty2<T> = [T] extends [[]] ? never : T" followed by "// never in, never out is the rule, not a bug" (and restated unqualified on page 4: "`never` in, `never` out — the empty union runs nothing"). Wrapping stops distribution, so the empty union is matched like any other type: `type A<T> = [T] extends [string] ? "yes" : "no"` gives `A<never> = "yes"`, not `never` — which is exactly why the `[T] extends [never]` idiom works.
findings.fix: Qualify the comment: "naked T only — `never` in, `never` out; wrapping in `[T]` stops distribution, so `never` is matched like any other type (that is how `[T] extends [never]` detects it)."
